question: What is Scrum?

options.text: A lightweight framework for generating value through adaptive solutions for complex problems
A predictive methodology that prescribes every design, test, and release step
A project-management process owned by a project manager
A set of engineering practices such as pair programming and continuous integration

explanation: Scrum is a lightweight framework, not a methodology or a prescribed engineering process. It helps people and teams generate value in complex work.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Purpose of the Scrum Guide

question: Scrum is founded on which pair of ideas?

options.text: Empiricism and lean thinking
Command-and-control and detailed upfront planning
Utilization targets and individual incentives
Fixed scope and variable quality

explanation: Empiricism says knowledge comes from experience and observation. Lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials.

question: Which are the three pillars of empirical process control?

options.text: Transparency
Inspection
Adaptation
Prediction
Utilization

explanation: Transparency, inspection, and adaptation are the pillars. Prediction and utilization are not Scrum pillars.

question: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.

options.text: True
False

explanation: People can inspect only what they can see. Hidden work makes inspection misleading.

question: Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless in Scrum.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Inspection is meant to detect undesirable variance so the team can adapt. Inspection that never leads to change does not serve empiricism.

question: Why do the Scrum artifacts matter for decision making?

options.text: Decisions to optimize value and control risk are based on the perceived state of the artifacts
Artifacts replace the need for stakeholder conversation
Artifacts are optional reports created at the end of a release
Artifacts exist so a project manager can assign tasks

explanation: If artifacts are not transparent, people may decide in ways that reduce value and increase risk.

question: Implementing only parts of Scrum still produces Scrum, as long as the team delivers something each month.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Scrum framework is immutable. Using only parts of it is possible, but the result is not Scrum.

question: Scrum events exist primarily to do what?

options.text: Create regularity and provide formal opportunities to inspect and adapt
Give management a weekly status forum
Replace the need for a Product Goal
Approve the Increment before it can be released

explanation: Events create a cadence and minimize the need for meetings that Scrum does not define. Skipping an event loses a chance to inspect and adapt.

question: Which are Scrum values?

options.text: Commitment
Focus
Openness
Respect
Courage
Obedience

explanation: The five Scrum values are commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage. Obedience is not one of them.

question: What does commitment mean in Scrum?

options.text: The Scrum Team commits to achieving its goals and to supporting each other
Developers sign a contract to finish every selected Product Backlog item
The Product Owner commits stakeholders to a fixed release date
The Scrum Master commits to remove every impediment personally

explanation: Commitment is to the goals and to each other. It is not a guarantee that every forecasted Product Backlog item will be finished.

question: Focus, as a Scrum value, means the Scrum Team primarily focuses on what?

options.text: The work of the Sprint, so it can make the best possible progress toward its goals
Keeping every stakeholder request inside the current Sprint
Maximizing individual utilization
Protecting the original Sprint Backlog from any new learning

explanation: The primary focus is the work of the Sprint and progress toward the Scrum Team’s goals.

question: Why do the Scrum values matter to empiricism?

options.text: When the team lives them, the pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life and trust is built
They replace the need for a Definition of Done
They let the team skip Sprint events when trust is high
They are optional cultural extras with no effect on the framework

explanation: Successful use of Scrum depends on people becoming more proficient in living the five values. Those values make empiricism real.

question: Which accountabilities exist inside a Scrum Team?

options.text: Product Owner
Scrum Master
Developers
Project manager
Business analyst as a separate accountability

explanation: The Scrum Guide defines three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers. It does not define a project manager or a separate analyst accountability.

question: A Scrum Team has no sub-teams or hierarchies.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Scrum Team is a cohesive unit of professionals with no sub-teams, such as a testing team, and no hierarchy among Developers.

question: In the 2020 Scrum Guide, self-managing means the team internally decides what?

options.text: Who does what, when, and how
Which Product Goal the organization must fund
The company-wide release policy without the Product Owner
That Sprint events are optional

explanation: The 2020 guide uses self-managing: the team decides who does what, when, and how. It does not use the older phrase self-organizing as the definition.

question: What does cross-functional mean for a Scrum Team?

options.text: The team as a whole has all the skills needed to create value each Sprint
Every person must be able to do every job equally well
Specialists stay in separate functional teams and hand work over
Only Developers need skills; the Product Owner and Scrum Master do not count

explanation: Cross-functional describes the team, not a requirement that every member has every skill.

question: The typical Scrum Team size is:

options.text: 10 or fewer people
At least 15 people so every specialty is represented
Exactly 7 plus or minus 2, as a hard rule
Whatever a resource manager assigns for the quarter

explanation: The team should be small enough to stay nimble and large enough to finish significant work, typically 10 or fewer.

question: Who is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint?

options.text: The entire Scrum Team
Only the Developers
Only the Product Owner
The Scrum Master

explanation: Developers create the Increment, and the Product Owner maximizes value, but the Scrum Guide holds the whole Scrum Team accountable for a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.

question: What can a product be, according to Scrum?

options.text: A service, a physical product, or something more abstract, with a clear boundary and known stakeholders
Only a software application
Only a project with a fixed end date
A backlog of stakeholder requests with no users

explanation: A product is a vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, and well-defined users or customers. It need not be software.

question: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product and for what else?

options.text: Effective Product Backlog management
Assigning daily tasks to Developers
Facilitating every Daily Scrum
Writing the Definition of Done alone

explanation: The Product Owner maximizes product value and is accountable for effective Product Backlog management, including the Product Goal, items, order, and transparency.

question: The Product Owner may be a committee if every stakeholder gets a vote on ordering.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. A committee may influence the Product Owner, but people who want the backlog changed must address that one person.

question: The Product Owner delegates Product Backlog refinement to Developers. Who remains accountable?

options.text: The Product Owner
The Developers who did the refinement
The Scrum Master, because facilitation was involved
Whoever has the most senior job title

explanation: The Product Owner may do backlog management or delegate the responsibility. Accountability stays with the Product Owner.

question: Who has the authority to cancel a Sprint?

options.text: Only the Product Owner
Only the Scrum Master
Any Developer, when the forecast looks wrong
The stakeholders, by majority vote

explanation: Only the Product Owner may cancel a Sprint, and only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Others may influence that decision.

question: For the Product Owner to succeed, the organization must do what?

options.text: Respect the Product Owner’s decisions, which are visible in the Product Backlog and the Increment
Let stakeholders reorder the Product Backlog during the Daily Scrum
Require a steering committee to approve every backlog change
Move Product Owner decisions to the Scrum Master

explanation: Product Owner decisions show up in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog and in the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review.

question: During Sprint Planning, how does the Product Owner contribute to the Sprint Goal?

options.text: The Product Owner proposes how the Sprint can increase value, then the whole Scrum Team collaborates on the Sprint Goal
The Product Owner writes the Sprint Goal alone and hands it to Developers
Developers pick a Sprint Goal and the Product Owner is informed afterward
Stakeholders vote on the Sprint Goal without the Scrum Team

explanation: The Product Owner proposes why the Sprint is valuable. The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal, which must be finalized before Sprint Planning ends.

question: The Scrum Master is accountable for what?

options.text: The Scrum Team’s effectiveness
The commercial budget of the product
Personally delivering the Increment
Ordering the Product Backlog

explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team’s effectiveness by helping it improve its practices within the Scrum framework.

question: How does the 2020 Scrum Guide describe Scrum Masters?

options.text: True leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization
People managers who assign tasks and rate individual performance
Meeting schedulers with no accountability for effectiveness
The only people allowed to talk to stakeholders

explanation: Scrum Masters are true leaders who serve. The guide no longer uses “servant-leader” as the defining phrase, but the service remains.

question: What does “causing removal of impediments” mean?

options.text: The Scrum Master is accountable for causing impediments to be removed, not necessarily for personally fixing every one
The Scrum Master must resolve every impediment before the next Daily Scrum
Developers are forbidden from removing their own impediments
Impediments can be removed only by a manager

explanation: The Scrum Master causes removal of impediments to the Scrum Team’s progress. Developers still solve problems they can handle themselves.

question: Which services does the Scrum Master provide to the organization?

options.text: Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption
Planning and advising Scrum implementations
Helping employees and stakeholders understand an empirical approach
Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams
Assigning Developers to Product Backlog items

explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organization through adoption, implementation advice, empiricism, and removing barriers. Assigning work is not that service.

question: The Scrum Master is required to assign tasks during Sprint Planning.

options.text: True
False

explanation: How the selected work is turned into an Increment is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No one else tells them how.

question: May a Scrum Master also do work in the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: Yes. If they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they participate in the Daily Scrum as a Developer
No. The Scrum Master is forbidden from creating any part of the Increment
Yes, but only the Product Owner may then attend the Daily Scrum
No, because a person cannot hold more than one skill

explanation: A Scrum Master may also be a Developer. When actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they participate in the Daily Scrum as a Developer.

question: Developers are always accountable for which of the following?

options.text: Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog
Instilling quality by adhering to the Definition of Done
Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal
Holding each other accountable as professionals
Ordering the Product Backlog for the Product Owner

explanation: Those four accountabilities belong to the Developers. Ordering the Product Backlog remains the Product Owner’s accountability.

question: Who selects how much Product Backlog work can be done in a Sprint?

options.text: The Developers, through discussion with the Product Owner
The Product Owner, who pushes a fixed scope into the Sprint
The Scrum Master, based on last Sprint’s velocity
Stakeholders at the Sprint Review

explanation: Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select the items. Their forecast is informed by past performance, upcoming capacity, and the Definition of Done.

question: Who is responsible for sizing Product Backlog items?

options.text: The Developers who will do the work
The Product Owner alone
The Scrum Master, using a mandated pointing scale
An external estimating office

explanation: The Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing. The Product Owner may help them understand trade-offs.

question: Who decides how to turn Product Backlog items into an Increment of value?

options.text: The Developers, at their sole discretion
The Product Owner, because they own the value decision
The Scrum Master, because they own the process
The architecture review board outside the Scrum Team

explanation: No one else tells the Developers how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

question: Which events does Scrum define?

options.text: The Sprint
Sprint Planning
Daily Scrum
Sprint Review
Sprint Retrospective
Backlog refinement as a mandatory event

explanation: The Sprint contains Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review, and the Sprint Retrospective. Refinement is an ongoing activity, not a required event.

question: Failing to hold a prescribed Scrum event reduces transparency and is a lost opportunity to inspect and adapt.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Each event is a formal chance to inspect and adapt. Omitting one reduces transparency.

question: How should event timeboxes change for a Sprint shorter than one month?

options.text: Sprint Planning, the Sprint Review, and the Sprint Retrospective are usually shorter. The Daily Scrum stays 15 minutes
Every event, including the Daily Scrum, must be cut exactly in half
Timeboxes stay at the one-month maximum even for a one-week Sprint
The Daily Scrum becomes optional

explanation: The guide says Planning, Review, and Retrospective are usually shorter for shorter Sprints. The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event regardless.

question: What is the maximum length of a Sprint?

options.text: One month
Six weeks, if the team agrees
Until the selected Product Backlog items are Done
One quarter

explanation: A Sprint is one month or less. A longer horizon makes the Sprint Goal less reliable and increases risk.

question: Once a Sprint begins, its duration is fixed and cannot be shortened or lengthened.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The timebox does not grow to finish leftover work and does not shrink just because the work finished early. Cancellation is the exception, and it is not used to end a successful Sprint early.

question: A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous Sprint ends.

options.text: True
False

explanation: There is no gap between Sprints. The next Sprint starts right away.

question: Which statements describe work during a Sprint?

options.text: No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal
Quality does not decrease
The Product Backlog is refined as needed
Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned
The Sprint Goal is rewritten whenever a new request arrives

explanation: Those four rules protect the Sprint. The Sprint Goal is not rewritten to absorb new requests; if it becomes obsolete, the Product Owner may cancel the Sprint.

question: The Developers finish the Sprint Goal early. What should happen?

options.text: The Sprint continues until the timebox ends. They may collaborate with the Product Owner about further work
The Sprint ends immediately so the next Sprint can start
The Definition of Done is weakened so more items can be called Done
Stakeholders extend the Sprint to pull in extra scope without negotiation

explanation: Finishing early does not end the Sprint. The duration stays fixed, and the team can pull further work with the Product Owner.

question: A Sprint is cancelled. What happens to the work?

options.text: Done items are reviewed. Incomplete items are re-estimated and returned to the Product Backlog
All unfinished items move automatically into the next Sprint
The Increment is discarded because the Sprint Goal was not met
The Scrum Master rewrites the Sprint Goal and continues the same Sprint

explanation: Cancellation is uncommon and costly. Completed work is still reviewed, and incomplete items go back to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

question: What is the timebox for Sprint Planning in a one-month Sprint?

options.text: A maximum of eight hours
Exactly eight hours, even if the team is done
Four hours
There is no timebox

explanation: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint. It is usually shorter for shorter Sprints.

question: Sprint Planning addresses which topics?

options.text: Why is this Sprint valuable?
What can be Done this Sprint?
How will the chosen work get done?
Which individuals failed last Sprint?

explanation: The three topics are why the Sprint is valuable, what can be Done, and how the chosen work will get done. Individual performance review is not a Sprint Planning topic.

question: The Sprint Goal must be finalized before Sprint Planning ends.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Sprint Goal is created during Sprint Planning and must be finalized before the event ends. It is then part of the Sprint Backlog.

question: Who may be invited to Sprint Planning besides the Scrum Team?

options.text: Other people, to provide advice
Only the Product Owner’s manager, who must approve the Sprint Goal
No one. The event is closed even for advice
Customers, who select the Sprint Backlog for the Developers

explanation: The Scrum Team may invite others to Sprint Planning to provide advice. Those guests do not take the Developers’ planning accountability.

question: What improves the Developers’ confidence in their Sprint forecast?

options.text: Knowing their past performance, upcoming capacity, and Definition of Done
A mandated velocity number from the Scrum Master
A fixed story-point quota
Ignoring the Definition of Done until the Sprint Review

explanation: Scrum does not require velocity or story points. Confidence comes from past performance, capacity, and a shared Definition of Done.

question: What is the Daily Scrum?

options.text: A 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team
A status meeting led by the Product Owner
A stakeholder demo held every day
A problem-solving workshop with no timebox

explanation: The Daily Scrum is 15 minutes, for the Developers, held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint to reduce complexity.

question: The three questions (what I did, what I will do, and my impediments) are mandatory in the Daily Scrum.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The 2020 Scrum Guide does not require the three questions. Developers choose any structure that focuses on the Sprint Goal and produces a plan for the next day.

question: When do the Product Owner and Scrum Master participate in the Daily Scrum?

options.text: When they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they participate as Developers
They must attend every Daily Scrum to receive a status report
They attend only when stakeholders are also present
They never attend, even if they are doing Sprint work

explanation: The Daily Scrum is for the Developers. The Product Owner or Scrum Master joins as a Developer only when actively working on Sprint Backlog items.

question: The Daily Scrum is the only time Developers are allowed to adjust their plan.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Developers often meet throughout the day for more detailed adaptation. The Daily Scrum is not the only moment the plan can change.

question: A good Daily Scrum produces what?

options.text: An actionable plan for the next day of work toward the Sprint Goal
A signed status report for the Product Owner
A revised Sprint Goal
A new Definition of Done

explanation: The Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and produce an actionable plan for the next day. That improves focus and self-management.

question: What is the timebox of the Sprint Review for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: A maximum of four hours
A maximum of three hours
Fifteen minutes
Eight hours

explanation: The Sprint Review is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint, and it is usually shorter for shorter Sprints.

question: Who takes part in the Sprint Review?

options.text: The Scrum Team and stakeholders
Only the Developers
Only the Product Owner and the stakeholders
Only the Scrum Master

explanation: The Scrum Team and key stakeholders inspect the outcome of the Sprint and progress toward the Product Goal.

question: The Sprint Review should be limited to a slide presentation.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session. The Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.

question: The Sprint Review is a gate: an Increment cannot be released until the Review is over.

options.text: True
False

explanation: A Done Increment may be delivered before the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Review should never be treated as a gate to releasing value.

question: Work that does not meet the Definition of Done may be:

options.text: Returned to the Product Backlog. It cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review
Presented as part of the Increment if the Product Owner accepts the risk
Released with a note that testing will follow next Sprint
Counted in the Increment because the Sprint timebox ended

explanation: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review. It returns to the Product Backlog.

question: What is the timebox of the Sprint Retrospective for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: A maximum of three hours
A maximum of four hours
Fifteen minutes
Eight hours

explanation: The Retrospective is timeboxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint and is usually shorter otherwise.

question: What is the purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: To plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness
To demo the Increment to stakeholders
To reorder the Product Backlog
To assign individual performance ratings

explanation: The Scrum Team inspects how the last Sprint went and plans improvements to quality and effectiveness.

question: The Sprint Retrospective inspects the last Sprint with regard to which topics?

options.text: Individuals
Interactions
Processes and tools
The Definition of Done
Individual salary decisions

explanation: The team inspects individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and their Definition of Done. Compensation decisions are not part of the event.

question: What may the Scrum Team do with the most impactful improvement?

options.text: Address it as soon as possible, and even add it to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint
Store it until a hardening Sprint
Hand it to a separate process-improvement team
Wait for the Product Owner to cancel a Sprint

explanation: The most impactful improvements are addressed as soon as possible. They may be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint. The Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

question: What is the Product Backlog?

options.text: An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product, and the single source of work for the Scrum Team
A fixed requirements document signed before the first Sprint
The plan for the current Sprint only
A list of tasks assigned to individuals

explanation: The Product Backlog is emergent and ordered. It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.

question: What is the commitment for the Product Backlog?

options.text: The Product Goal
The Sprint Goal
The Definition of Done
A release burndown

explanation: Each artifact has a commitment. The Product Backlog’s commitment is the Product Goal. The Sprint Goal belongs to the Sprint Backlog, and the Definition of Done belongs to the Increment.

question: A Scrum Team should pursue several Product Goals at the same time so stakeholders have more options.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The Scrum Team fulfills or abandons one Product Goal before taking on the next. The Product Goal is the long-term objective and lives in the Product Backlog.

question: Product Backlog refinement is a mandatory Scrum event with its own timebox.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Refinement is the ongoing act of breaking down and further defining items, adding details such as description, order, and size. It is not one of the Scrum events.

question: Scrum requires a Definition of Ready before a Product Backlog item can enter Sprint Planning.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Scrum requires a Definition of Done, not a Definition of Ready. An item is ready for selection when the Scrum Team can get it Done within one Sprint, usually after refinement.

question: The Sprint Backlog is composed of which three things?

options.text: The Sprint Goal, the selected Product Backlog items, and the plan for delivering them
The Product Goal, the Definition of Done, and a release date
A task list, a velocity target, and a risk log
Only the Product Backlog items the Product Owner assigned

explanation: The Sprint Goal, the selected items, and the delivery plan together are the Sprint Backlog.

question: What is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog?

options.text: The Sprint Goal
The list of selected Product Backlog items
The Product Goal
The Definition of Done

explanation: The Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog. It is a single objective and gives flexibility about the exact work needed.

question: Who can change the Sprint Backlog during the Sprint?

options.text: The Developers. Scope changes are negotiated with the Product Owner without affecting the Sprint Goal
Only the Product Owner
Only the Scrum Master
Any stakeholder who attends the Daily Scrum

explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. They update it as they learn. Scope can be renegotiated with the Product Owner if the Sprint Goal stays intact.

question: The Sprint Goal becomes obsolete midway through the Sprint. What is the appropriate Scrum response?

options.text: The Product Owner may cancel the Sprint
The Developers rewrite the Sprint Goal and continue
The Scrum Master extends the Sprint
The team weakens the Definition of Done and keeps the original Goal

explanation: The Sprint Goal does not change during the Sprint. If it is obsolete, only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

question: When is an Increment born?

options.text: The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done
When the Sprint Review starts
When a stakeholder says the demo looked good
When the Sprint timebox ends, whether or not the work is Done

explanation: An Increment is born when a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done. It must be usable.

question: More than one Increment can be created during a Sprint.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint. Their sum is presented at the Sprint Review so that all the work supports one another.

question: What must be true of an Increment?

options.text: It is usable and additive to all prior Increments, which have been thoroughly verified so they work together
It is potentially releasable only after a separate hardening Sprint
It may exclude testing if the Definition of Done is updated at the Review
It is a document describing work that will be built later

explanation: Each Increment is additive to prior Increments and thoroughly verified. To provide value, it must be usable.

question: A team wants a hardening Sprint after three feature Sprints so testing can catch up. What does Scrum say?

options.text: There is no hardening Sprint. Every Sprint must produce a Done, usable Increment
A hardening Sprint is required once quality work is deferred
Sprint 0 creates the Increment, and later Sprints only add features
Testing is a Scrum event that happens after the Retrospective

explanation: Quality does not decrease, and undone work is not part of the Increment. Scrum has no Sprint 0 or hardening Sprint. Work required by the Definition of Done happens in the Sprint.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — The Sprint and Increment

question: The Definition of Done is the commitment for which artifact?

options.text: The Increment
The Product Backlog
The Sprint Backlog
The Sprint Goal

explanation: The Definition of Done is the commitment for the Increment. It is a formal description of the quality measures required for the product.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Commitment: Definition of Done

question: The organization already has a Definition of Done. What must the Scrum Team do?

options.text: Follow it as a minimum. The team may make it stricter
Ignore it and write a private Definition of Done
Use it only for the Sprint Review demo
Replace it with each Developer’s personal checklist

explanation: If the Definition of Done is an organizational standard, every Scrum Team must follow it at least. If it is not, the Scrum Team must create one appropriate for the product.

question: Several Scrum Teams work on one product. Which Definition of Done applies?

options.text: They must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done
Each team keeps a private Definition of Done
Only the integration team needs a Definition of Done
The Product Owner chooses a different one per Sprint

explanation: Multiple Scrum Teams on the same product share one Definition of Done so their Increments fit together. Developers must conform to it.

question: Developers may weaken the Definition of Done during a Sprint so the forecast can be called complete.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Quality does not decrease during the Sprint. Lowering the Definition of Done to meet a date violates that rule.

question: A Scrum Team grows too large. What does the Scrum Guide suggest?

options.text: Reorganize into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams on the same product, sharing the Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner
Add a project manager layer above the Developers
Split the Product Backlog so each team has its own Product Owner and Product Goal
Create a separate testing team that receives work after each Sprint

explanation: If a team is too large, it should consider multiple cohesive Scrum Teams focused on the same product. They share the Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

question: Which statements are true when multiple Scrum Teams work on one product?

options.text: They share one Product Owner
They share one Product Backlog
They share one Product Goal
They mutually define and follow the same Definition of Done
Each team must have its own Product Owner

explanation: One product means one Product Owner, one Product Backlog, and one Product Goal. Teams on that product also share a Definition of Done.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — The Scrum Team and Definition of Done

question: Which complementary practices does Scrum require?

options.text: None. Velocity, burndown charts, and user stories may be used, but Scrum does not require them
Story points and planning poker
A release burndown owned by the Scrum Master
User stories with a mandatory template

explanation: Scrum is purposefully incomplete. Velocity, burndown charts, and user stories are complementary practices, not framework requirements.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Purpose of the Scrum Guide

question: A person is asked to be both Product Owner and Scrum Master for the same team. What is the best description?

options.text: The Scrum Guide does not forbid it, but the accountabilities can conflict, so it is generally unwise
Scrum forbids one person from holding both accountabilities
It is the recommended pattern because it shortens communication
It is allowed only if stakeholders approve the Sprint Goal

explanation: The accountabilities are distinct. Combining them can undermine the balance between value decisions and team effectiveness. The guide does not state an explicit ban.

question: A tester and a business analyst create the Increment with the other Developers. What are their Scrum accountabilities?

options.text: Developers. Scrum does not create separate tester or analyst accountabilities
A QA accountability and a business-analyst accountability
Stakeholders, because they do not write production code
Scrum Masters, because they improve quality and clarity

explanation: People doing the work of creating a usable Increment are Developers, regardless of their specialist titles. There are only three accountabilities.

question: Why does Scrum prescribe formal events?

options.text: To create regularity and to minimize the need for meetings not defined in Scrum
To give each accountability a private status meeting
To delay adaptation until the end of the month
To replace transparency of the artifacts

explanation: The events create a steady cadence. Optimally they are held at the same time and place to reduce complexity.

question: Adaptation becomes more difficult when:

options.text: The people involved are not empowered or self-managing
The Scrum Team inspects a transparent Increment
The Definition of Done is shared
The Sprint Goal is clear

explanation: A Scrum Team is expected to adapt as soon as it learns something through inspection. That is harder when people are not empowered or self-managing.

question: Who is accountable for the order of the Product Backlog?

options.text: The Product Owner
The Developers, because they size the work
The Scrum Master
The stakeholders collectively

explanation: Ordering Product Backlog items is part of Product Backlog management. The Product Owner is accountable, even when others help with the work.

question: The Scrum Master notices the Daily Scrum regularly runs past 15 minutes. What is an appropriate response?

options.text: Teach the Developers to keep the event focused and inside the timebox
Take over the event and collect a status from each person
Cancel the Daily Scrum until the team is more experienced
Extend the timebox to 30 minutes in the working agreement

explanation: The Scrum Master ensures Scrum events happen, stay positive and productive, and remain within the timebox. The Daily Scrum still belongs to the Developers.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Scrum Master and Daily Scrum

question: Progress toward the Product Goal is discussed primarily at which event?

options.text: The Sprint Review
The Daily Scrum
A management status meeting outside Scrum
Sprint Planning topic three only

explanation: At the Sprint Review, the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome and discuss progress toward the Product Goal. The Daily Scrum focuses on the Sprint Goal.

question: The Sprint Goal is a commitment by whom, and what flexibility does it create?

options.text: A commitment by the Developers that still allows flexibility in the exact work needed to achieve it
A commitment by stakeholders that every selected item will be delivered
A commitment by the Scrum Master that no impediments will occur
A commitment that freezes the Sprint Backlog

explanation: The Sprint Goal is a commitment by the Developers. It creates coherence and focus while leaving room to adjust the exact work with the Product Owner.

question: A Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges ahead. Which Scrum value does this illustrate?

options.text: Openness
Commitment
Focus
Respect

explanation: Openness means the Scrum Team and its stakeholders are transparent about the work and the challenges ahead.

question: Why does the Scrum Guide describe the framework as purposefully incomplete?

options.text: Because the Guide is still being written
Because only certified coaches know the missing parts
Because it defines only the parts required to implement Scrum theory, while teams may use various processes, techniques, and methods within it
Because teams are expected to skip the events they find unnecessary

explanation: Scrum is purposefully incomplete. It relies on the collective intelligence of the people using it, and its rules guide relationships and interactions rather than giving detailed instructions.

question: Which of the following are part of effective Product Backlog management?

options.text: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal
Ordering Product Backlog items
Sizing every Product Backlog item on behalf of the Developers
Ensuring the Product Backlog is transparent, visible, and understood

explanation: Effective Product Backlog management also includes creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items. Sizing is the Developers' responsibility.

question: How can someone who wants a change in the Product Backlog get it made?

options.text: By editing the Product Backlog directly
By trying to convince the Product Owner
By voting during the Sprint Review
By asking the Scrum Master to reorder it

explanation: People who want to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner. The organization must respect those decisions.

question: What is the Scrum Master accountable for regarding Scrum itself?

options.text: Ordering the Product Backlog
Establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide, by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice
Personally delivering the Increment each Sprint
Managing performance reviews of the Developers

explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide. Helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, inside the team and the organization, is how that accountability is carried out.

question: Which of the following are ways the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner?

options.text: Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management
Helping the Scrum Team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items
Ordering the Product Backlog
Facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed

explanation: The Scrum Master also helps establish empirical product planning for a complex environment. Ordering the Product Backlog stays with the Product Owner.

question: Which statement about the Scrum Master and Scrum events is correct?

options.text: The Scrum Master must personally facilitate every event
The Scrum Master ensures that all Scrum events take place and are positive, productive, and kept within the timebox
The Scrum Master decides which events can be skipped
The Scrum Master attends only the Sprint Retrospective

explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for the events happening and staying productive and timeboxed. That does not require the Scrum Master to run each event personally.

question: Why are shorter Sprints useful?

options.text: They shorten the learning cycle and limit the risk of cost and effort to a smaller time frame
They remove the need for a Product Owner
They eliminate the Sprint Retrospective
They guarantee that the Product Goal is reached sooner

explanation: Shorter Sprints generate more learning cycles and limit risk. A longer Sprint can make the Sprint Goal invalid, and complexity and risk grow with the length.

question: What does the Scrum Guide say about burn-downs, burn-ups, and cumulative flow?

options.text: They replace empiricism
They are forbidden in Scrum
They can be useful, but they do not replace the importance of empiricism
They are mandatory in the Sprint Review

explanation: Various practices exist to forecast progress, such as burn-downs, burn-ups, or cumulative flows. In complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decisions.

question: What does the Product Owner do to prepare Sprint Planning?

options.text: Estimate every item for the Developers
Assign each item to an individual Developer
Ensure that attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal
Write the plan for how the chosen work will be done

explanation: The Product Owner ensures attendees are ready to discuss the most important items and how they relate to the Product Goal. The Scrum Team may also invite other people to provide advice.

question: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?

options.text: To report status to the Scrum Master
To update management on progress
To inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary
To plan the next Sprint

explanation: The Daily Scrum inspects progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapts the Sprint Backlog, adjusting the upcoming planned work.

question: What is the purpose of the Sprint Review?

options.text: To approve the Increment before it can be released
To evaluate individual performance
To inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations
To plan each Developer's tasks for the next Sprint

explanation: The Scrum Team presents the results of its work to key stakeholders and discusses progress toward the Product Goal. The Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities.

question: Which event concludes the Sprint?

options.text: The Sprint Review
The Daily Scrum
Sprint Planning
The Sprint Retrospective

explanation: The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint. The Sprint Review is the second-to-last event.

question: Which Product Backlog items are ready for selection in Sprint Planning?

options.text: Those the Scrum Team can get Done within one Sprint
Those estimated above 13 points
Every item currently in the Product Backlog
Those a stakeholder committee has approved

explanation: Product Backlog items that the Scrum Team can complete within one Sprint are ready for selection in Sprint Planning. They usually reach that transparency through refinement. Scrum does not require a separate Definition of Ready.

question: What is the Product Goal?

options.text: The objective of a single Sprint
A checklist of quality criteria for the Increment
The Developers’ plan for the current Sprint
The long-term objective for the Scrum Team, describing a future state of the product that serves as a target for planning

explanation: The Product Goal is the commitment for the Product Backlog and lives in it. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define what will fulfill that goal. The Scrum Team must fulfill or abandon one Product Goal before taking on another.

question: What is the Definition of Done?

options.text: The task list for the current Sprint
A contract between the Product Owner and the stakeholders
A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product
A checklist owned only by the Scrum Master

explanation: The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born. The Definition of Done creates transparency by giving everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Commitment: Definition of Done

question: What did the 2020 Scrum Guide change about how a Scrum Team manages its work?

options.text: It keeps a self-organizing Development Team inside the Scrum Team
It describes one self-managing Scrum Team, which chooses who, how, and what to work on
It lets management assign the Sprint work
It lets the Scrum Master assign the Sprint work

explanation: Earlier Scrum Guides described self-organizing Development Teams. The 2020 Guide describes a self-managing Scrum Team that chooses who, how, and what to work on.

question: Which commitment did the 2020 Scrum Guide introduce?

options.text: The Product Goal
The Sprint Goal
The Definition of Done
Velocity

explanation: The 2020 Guide introduces the Product Goal, so each Sprint moves the product toward a larger objective. The Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done already existed, and each commitment is now tied to an artifact.

question: What does empiricism assert?

options.text: Knowledge comes from experience, and decisions are based on what is observed
Knowledge comes from a detailed plan written before the work starts
Decisions should wait until every risk has been predicted
The best decision is the one made by the most senior job title

explanation: Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and from making decisions based on what is observed. Scrum pairs that idea with lean thinking.

question: Why does Scrum use an iterative, incremental approach?

options.text: To optimize predictability and to control risk
To remove the need for inspection
To fix the scope before the first Sprint
To guarantee a release date

explanation: An iterative, incremental approach optimizes predictability and controls risk. It does not remove inspection or freeze scope up front.

question: Who must be able to see the emergent process and the work?

options.text: The people performing the work and the people receiving the work
Only the Product Owner
Only the Scrum Master
Only the stakeholders who attend the Sprint Review

explanation: Transparency means the emergent process and work are visible to those performing the work and to those receiving it. Important decisions are based on the perceived state of the artifacts.

question: What can artifacts with low transparency lead to?

options.text: Decisions that diminish value and increase risk
Faster adaptation, because less information is discussed
A stronger Sprint Goal
Automatic cancellation of the Sprint

explanation: Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk. The artifacts exist so everyone inspecting them shares a basis for adaptation.

question: How should inspection be timed?

options.text: Frequently and diligently enough to detect problems, without happening so often that inspection gets in the way of the work
Only at the Sprint Review
Continuously, even when it stops the Developers from creating the Increment
Only when the Scrum Master requests it

explanation: The artifacts and the progress toward agreed goals are inspected frequently and diligently. Scrum events provide that cadence. Inspection should not be so frequent that it gets in the way of the work.

question: A process has drifted outside acceptable limits, or the resulting product is unacceptable. When is the adjustment made?

options.text: As soon as possible, to minimize further deviation
At the next quarterly planning meeting
After the Product Goal is already achieved
Only after the Scrum Master approves a written change request

explanation: If any aspect of a process deviates outside acceptable limits, or the resulting product is unacceptable, the process or the materials being produced must be adjusted. The adjustment is made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation.

question: What does respect mean as a Scrum value?

options.text: Scrum Team members respect each other as capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people they work with
The team defers every decision to the most senior person
Stakeholders accept the Product Backlog and do not discuss it
Respect replaces the need for a Definition of Done

explanation: Respect means team members regard each other as capable, independent people, and the people they work with regard them the same way.

question: What does courage mean as a Scrum value?

options.text: Scrum Team members have the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems
The team delays difficult Product Backlog items until a later release
Problems stay private until the Sprint Review
The Scrum Master decides which problems are safe to discuss

explanation: Courage means the Scrum Team members do the right thing and work on tough problems.

question: How should the decisions of a Scrum Team relate to the Scrum values?

options.text: The decisions, the steps taken, and the way Scrum is used should reinforce the values, not diminish or undermine them
The values apply only during the Sprint Retrospective
The values can be set aside when a deadline is close
The values replace the Sprint Goal

explanation: The values give direction to the work, actions, and behavior of the Scrum Team. Decisions and the way Scrum is used should reinforce those values, not diminish or undermine them.

question: Which of the following are product-related activities a Scrum Team can be responsible for?

options.text: Stakeholder collaboration
Verification, maintenance, and operation
Experimentation, research, and development
A project manager assigning each Developer a daily task

explanation: The Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities, from stakeholder collaboration through verification, maintenance, operation, experimentation, research, and development, and anything else required. The organization structures and empowers the team to manage its own work.

question: What does the Scrum Guide say about the skills Developers need?

options.text: The specific skills needed are often broad and vary with the domain of work
Every Developer must be able to perform every task
Only software programmers can be Developers
The Scrum Master assigns one specialty to each Developer

explanation: Developers are the people committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint. The specific skills needed are often broad and vary with the domain of work.

question: How can the needs of many stakeholders be reflected in the Product Backlog?

options.text: The Product Owner may represent those needs in the Product Backlog
Each stakeholder adds and reorders items directly
The stakeholders vote during the Daily Scrum and override the Product Owner
The stakeholders and the Scrum Master form a Product Owner committee

explanation: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee, and may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog. People who want a change try to convince the Product Owner.

question: Which of the following is a way the Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team?

options.text: Coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality
Assigning tasks to individual Developers
Ordering the Product Backlog
Writing a hidden Definition of Done and keeping it from the Developers

explanation: The Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team by coaching self-management and cross-functionality, helping the team focus on high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done, causing impediments to be removed, and ensuring the Scrum events take place and stay within the timebox.

question: What does the Scrum Guide say about the time and place of the Scrum events?

options.text: Optimally, all events are held at the same time and place to reduce complexity
Each event must be held in a different place
The Scrum Master chooses a new time for every Sprint
An event may be skipped when the team already knows the status

explanation: Events create regularity and minimize the need for meetings that Scrum does not define. Optimally they are held at the same time and place to reduce complexity. Skipping a prescribed event is a lost opportunity to inspect and adapt.

question: How does the 2020 Scrum Guide describe a Sprint?

options.text: The heartbeat of Scrum, where ideas are turned into value, and the container for every other Scrum event
A project with a horizon of one month
A release phase that ends only when the Product Owner accepts the Increment
An optional planning cycle the team may skip

explanation: Sprints are the heartbeat of Scrum, where ideas are turned into value. The Sprint contains the other events. All the work needed to achieve the Product Goal, including Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrums, the Sprint Review, and the Sprint Retrospective, happens within Sprints.

question: The Developers forecast which Product Backlog items they can complete in the Sprint. Which statement matches the Scrum Guide?

options.text: The Sprint Goal is the commitment. Scope may be renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned
Every selected item becomes a commitment that must be finished or the Sprint has failed
Stakeholders may insert mandatory items during the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal
Unfinished items move automatically into the next Sprint

explanation: The Sprint Goal is the single objective and the commitment by the Developers. It leaves flexibility in the exact work. Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner without endangering the Sprint Goal. Unfinished items return to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

question: Who creates the plan that comes out of Sprint Planning?

options.text: The whole Scrum Team, working together
The Product Owner alone
The Scrum Master alone
The stakeholders, who then hand the plan to the Developers

explanation: Sprint Planning lays out the work for the Sprint. The resulting plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team.

question: How do Developers often break down the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint?

options.text: Into smaller work items of one day or less, in whatever way they choose
They wait for the Product Owner to assign the tasks
They follow a work-breakdown template required by the Scrum Guide
The Scrum Master sequences the tasks for them

explanation: For each selected item, the Developers plan the work needed to create an Increment that meets the Definition of Done. This is often done by decomposing items into smaller work of one day or less. How they do that is at their sole discretion. Nobody else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.

question: Why is the Daily Scrum held at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint?

options.text: To reduce complexity
So the Scrum Master can collect a status report
So stakeholders can attend a daily demonstration
Because the timebox changes from day to day

explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers. Holding it at the same time and place every working day of the Sprint reduces complexity.

question: Which outcome does the Scrum Guide associate with the Daily Scrum?

options.text: Clearer communication, visible impediments, quicker decisions, and less need for other meetings
A written status report for management
A rewritten Sprint Goal
A new Definition of Done

explanation: Daily Scrums improve communications, identify impediments, promote quick decision-making, and therefore eliminate the need for other meetings. The Developers may still meet through the day for more detailed replanning.

question: What may the attendees do during the Sprint Review after they inspect the Sprint outcome?

options.text: Collaborate on what to do next, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities
Have the Scrum Master accept or reject the Increment
Weaken the Definition of Done so unfinished work can be presented
Decompose the next Sprint into assigned tasks

explanation: The Scrum Team and stakeholders review what was accomplished and what has changed in their environment. They then collaborate on what to do next. The Product Backlog may be adjusted to meet new opportunities. The Review is a working session, not a gate for releasing value.

question: Which of the following does the Scrum Team discuss in the Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: What went well during the Sprint
Problems it ran into, and how those problems were or were not solved
Assumptions that led the team astray, and where those assumptions came from
Individual salary decisions

explanation: The team inspects how the last Sprint went and discusses what went well, the problems it encountered, and how those problems were or were not solved. Assumptions that led them astray are identified and their origins explored. The elements inspected often vary with the domain of work.

question: Which details does the Scrum Guide give as examples of what refinement may add to a Product Backlog item?

options.text: A description
Order
Size
A story-point value that Scrum requires

explanation: Refinement is the ongoing activity of breaking items down and defining them further, adding details such as a description, order, and size. Those attributes often vary with the domain of work. Scrum does not require story points.

question: Which description of the Sprint Backlog matches the Scrum Guide?

options.text: A highly visible, real-time picture of the planned work, updated as more is learned, with enough detail to inspect progress in the Daily Scrum
A fixed task list signed at the end of Sprint Planning
A plan owned by the Product Owner and changed only at the Sprint Review
A release schedule for the next quarter

explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work they plan in order to achieve the Sprint Goal, and it is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.

question: What is an Increment?

options.text: A concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal
A document that describes work planned for a later Sprint
Another name for the Sprint Backlog
A status report presented by the Scrum Master

explanation: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, so that all Increments work together. To provide value, the Increment must be usable.

question: Why is the sum of the Increments presented at the Sprint Review?

options.text: Presenting them supports empiricism
The Sprint Review is the only moment an Increment may be released
The presentation replaces the Definition of Done
The Scrum Master uses it to accept or reject the Increment

explanation: The sum of the Increments is presented at the Sprint Review, which supports empiricism. An Increment may still be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Review is not a gate to releasing value.

question: The organization has no standard Definition of Done. What must happen?

options.text: The Scrum Team creates a Definition of Done appropriate for the product
The team may release work with no shared quality measure
The Scrum Master writes a private checklist and does not share it
Each Developer uses a personal definition, and the result is still an Increment

explanation: If the Definition of Done is an organizational standard, all Scrum Teams follow it as a minimum. If it is not, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Commitment: Definition of Done

question: Who is required to conform to the Definition of Done?

options.text: The Developers
Only the Product Owner
Only the stakeholders at the Sprint Review
Only the Scrum Master

explanation: The Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done. If several Scrum Teams work on one product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Commitment: Definition of Done

question: Why does each Scrum artifact contain a commitment?

options.text: To reinforce empiricism and the Scrum values, and to provide a focus against which progress can be measured
To replace inspection and adaptation
To freeze the Product Backlog for the whole release
To give the Scrum Master a scale for rating individuals

explanation: Each artifact contains a commitment so that it provides information that enhances transparency and focus: the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal, and the Definition of Done. These commitments reinforce empiricism and the Scrum values.

question: How does the 2020 Scrum Guide refer to the Product Owner, the Scrum Master, and the Developers?

options.text: As three accountabilities within one Scrum Team
As three roles that form separate sub-teams
As three job titles assigned by a line manager
As a Development Team plus two managers

explanation: The 2020 Guide defines three accountabilities inside one Scrum Team: Developers, Product Owner, and Scrum Master. It no longer describes a separate Development Team inside the Scrum Team.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Scrum Team; Changes between 2017 and 2020
